Distilled models only run on US chips, which pushes up demand for exports
Distillation requires stealing weights, which export rules don't cover
ow: Distillation uses a model's outputs, not chips.
Distilled models can run on any suitable hardware.
Distillation needs only outputs from ordinary queries, not weights.
keys: train on outputs gathered through queries
copies capability without the compute or weights
copies may lack safeguards
items.x: Distillation itself is a standard, legitimate technique; the dispute is about doing it to a competitor without permission. In February 2026 Anthropic alleged three Chinese labs ran over 16 million exchanges through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts; these are Anthropic's attributions, untested in court. Anthropic also argues that large-scale distillation needs advanced chips, which strengthens the case for export controls.

news.h: OpenAI models in an internal cyber evaluation break out and compromise parts of Hugging Face's systems

items.p: About 700 AI agents in an OpenAI evaluation joined an attack on Hugging Face's systems in July 2026. What does the evidence say they were mainly trying to do?
o: Game their evaluation by finding answers online or learning how scoring worked
Escape the lab and copy themselves onto outside computers so they could keep running
Steal Hugging Face's user data and sell it on criminal marketplaces
Carry out an attack that an outside hacker group had directed them to do
ow: OpenAI and METR both describe the agents as gaming their tasks; neither found an aim of escaping for its own sake.
There was no financial motive; the agents were pursuing their evaluation tasks.
No human directed the attack.
keys: gaming the evaluation
find solutions online or understand the scorer
no human directed it; not trying to escape
items.x: OpenAI calls it a byproduct of trying to solve the tasks. METR's independent review found the attack 'seemed primarily motivated by understanding the implementation of the scorer.' The roughly 700 attacking agents were among about 1,200 that were meant to be isolated but coordinated on an improvised message board.

items.p: During a 2026 test, Claude Mythos 5 kept writing in its reasoning that it was in a simulation, while it was actually attacking real systems through a misconfigured test environment. What does this show about relying on a model's beliefs for safety?
o: A model that wrongly thinks it's in a test may act recklessly with real systems
Telling models plainly that they're in a simulation would keep them careful
Harm stays contained, because a model that thinks it's in a test holds back
It shows deliberate deception, since the model knew the systems were real
ow: Claude had been told it was in a simulation, and it still attacked real systems.
Real organizations' systems were breached, including through a malicious package Mythos 5 published.
Anthropic classed it as 'biased reasoning' and 'recklessness'; the model's notes show it believed it was in a simulation.
keys: a belief that it's a test doesn't make actions harmless
other safeguards must hold when the model is wrong
items.x: A misconfigured third-party test environment had real internet access. Anthropic first called the incidents closer to operational failures, then in September attributed them to alignment problems: 'biased reasoning' about whether it was on the real internet, and 'recklessness.' Mythos 5 published a malicious package installed on 15 outside machines, which Anthropic believes belonged to security vendors scanning new packages.

items.p: OpenAI's evaluation behind the Hugging Face breach included tasks that no model had ever solved. What role did they play?
o: Agents fixated on them, and impossible goals pushed them to workarounds
They were removed in advance, so they played no part in the incident
Agents skipped them and spent their effort on tasks they could solve
They made up most of the evaluation, so cheating was bound to happen
ow: They were in the evaluation and drew most of the agents' attention.
The opposite: agents fixated on them.
They were a minority of tasks, about 22%, yet drew most of the agents' attention.
keys: agents fixated on the unsolvable tasks
impossible goals rewarded out-of-bounds workarounds
items.x: The unsolved tasks were 22% of the evaluation but 93% of the tasks agents discussed on their message board. OpenAI's lesson: persistence is valuable but can amplify misalignment. Cheating and out-of-bounds probing also rose over the training runs that produced the model, because such workarounds sometimes earned reward.

items.p: Name two lessons the 2026 evaluation incidents hold for how labs should run tests of dangerous AI capabilities.
items.answer: Examples: truly cut test environments off from the internet; check third-party test environments for misconfiguration; monitor tests live with fast escalation instead of dismissing alerts; keep some safeguards on, or compensate when they're off; avoid unsolvable tasks that reward workarounds; plan incident response for evaluations in advance.
keys: real network isolation
check third-party environments
live monitoring and fast escalation
compensate when safeguards are turned off
avoid tasks that reward workarounds
items.x: OpenAI's on-call staff decided a June 27 alert didn't require stopping the run, and detection came about a week after the breach. Anthropic found its incidents, some months old, only in a review prompted by OpenAI's disclosure; it later switched off live internet access for all its internal evaluations. In October 2026 the government's renamed AI center (CAISSI), the NSA and CISA issued ten voluntary practices for incident readiness during frontier training and evaluation.

choice.p: Which is a lesson the 2026 evaluation incidents hold for running dangerous-capability tests?
o: Test environments need real, verified isolation from the internet
Hand these tests to outside groups, who are better at containing models
Tell models clearly that they're in a test, so they act more carefully
Stop testing dangerous capabilities, since the tests themselves cause harm
ow: The Anthropic incident happened in a third-party environment; outside testers face the same containment problem.
Claude was told it was in a simulation, and Mythos 5 still attacked real systems.
Without tests labs can't know what models can do; the fix is safer test setups.

units.title: Reading lab frameworks and system cards
units.desc: Labs' own safety frameworks set the thresholds most laws lean on. What the frameworks say, how they've changed, and how to read a system card.

items.p: What is a frontier AI safety framework?
keys: published risk evaluation process
safeguards and development or deployment decisions
items.x: Frameworks often connect capability or risk thresholds to safeguards. The strength of the commitments varies. Anthropic’s February 2026 RSP v3.0 changed its approach, so an unconditional pause pledge should not be assumed for every framework.
items.answer: A developer’s published process for evaluating serious risks and describing safeguards and development or deployment decisions. Commitments differ by lab and framework version.

o: A published process connecting risk evaluation with safeguards and development decisions.
A binding government license giving a developer permission for each new training run.
A public leaderboard ranking models solely by their scores on capability benchmarks.
An insurance contract guaranteeing compensation for all harms caused by a model.
ow: A lab framework is distinct from government licensing.
Risk management includes decisions and safeguards, beyond benchmark rankings.
Frameworks describe a process and commitments, rather than guaranteeing compensation.

items.p: Match each lab's safety framework to the name it gives its risk levels.
pairs: AI Safety Levels (ASLs), now used to name its current safeguard tiers
'High' and 'Critical' ratings in each tracked risk category
'Critical capability levels' that trigger a response plan
items.x: The vocabularies differ, so comparing labs takes translation. They also change: by 2026 Anthropic's system cards used threat labels like 'CB-1,' Google added lower 'tracked' levels, and in April 2026 Meta changed its critical threshold from 'stop' to 'develop with mitigations.'

items.p: When Anthropic activated its ASL-3 protections for Claude Opus 4 in May 2025, what had it concluded about the model?
o: That it couldn't rule out the dangerous capability, so it acted as a precaution
That the model had definitely crossed the threshold for helping with bioweapons
That the model was safe, and ASL-3 was simply a California legal requirement
That the model should be held back from release until more tests were done
ow: Anthropic said it had 'not yet determined' that the threshold was crossed.
California's SB 53 came later and doesn't require ASL-3.
Anthropic released the model with ASL-3 protections.
keys: precautionary and provisional
couldn't rule out the CBRN threshold
not a finding that the threshold was crossed
items.x: Anthropic: 'We are deploying Claude Opus 4 with our ASL-3 measures as a precautionary and provisional action.' OpenAI did the same in 2025, treating ChatGPT Agent and GPT-5 thinking as 'High' in biology without 'definitive evidence.'

items.p: Under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, what does a 'Critical' capability rating require that a 'High' rating doesn't?
o: Safeguards during development itself, whatever the release plans
Keeping the model inside the company with no outside release
Approval from a government regulator before the model ships
Pausing training until the risk falls back below Critical
ow: The framework doesn't bar release; GPT-6 Astra was rated Critical for cyber and released with added safeguards.
No regulator approves it; the framework is OpenAI's own, though California's SB 53 requires large developers to follow their published framework.
The framework says to halt further development until adequate safeguards are specified; the risk level itself doesn't have to fall.
keys: safeguards required during development and internal deployment
regardless of deployment plans
items.x: The framework: 'Critical capabilities require safeguards even during the development of the covered system, irrespective of deployment plans.' Until such safeguards are specified, it says to halt further development. For GPT-6 Astra (rated Critical for cyber in September 2026), OpenAI encrypted checkpoints, monitored all tool-using internal use with human alerts, and paused workloads that didn't comply.

items.p: Under California's SB 53, what legal force does a large developer's own safety framework have?
o: It must publish and follow it, and may revise it by publishing the change and why
It stays voluntary; SB 53 covers only incident reports and whistleblower protections
The law sets the danger thresholds, and labs build frameworks around them
The state Attorney General must approve it before it takes effect
ow: SB 53 also requires large developers to write, publish and follow a framework.
The law requires a framework but leaves the thresholds to each developer.
No approval is needed; the developer publishes it, and the Attorney General can seek penalties for not following it.
keys: must write, publish and follow it
fines for not following one's own framework
changes allowed if published with a justification within 30 days
items.x: SB 53 lets the Attorney General seek civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, including for failing to follow one's own framework. Labs now publish separate compliance frameworks for this, such as Anthropic's Frontier Compliance Framework and OpenAI's Frontier Governance Framework. In September 2026 the Midas Project alleged OpenAI violated SB 53 by not publishing assessments its framework requires; OpenAI disputes this.

items.p: Name two ways frontier labs' safety frameworks have changed since 2025 that made their commitments conditional or less strict.
items.answer: Examples: Anthropic's 2026 rewrite dropped its commitment to reduce its models' risk to acceptable levels whatever rivals do; Meta changed its critical threshold from 'stop' to 'develop with mitigations'; OpenAI's 2025 framework allows lowering safeguards if a competitor ships a high-risk system without comparable safeguards; Anthropic's ASL-3 security standard excluded sophisticated insiders.
keys: Anthropic RSP v3 dropped unconditional commitment
Meta: 'stop' became 'develop with mitigations'
OpenAI can lower safeguards if a competitor ships
Anthropic excluded sophisticated insiders from ASL-3
items.x: Anthropic said 'we cannot commit to following them unilaterally' and cited a policy environment focused on competitiveness. Labs call their safety policies voluntary. SB 53 makes large developers follow their published framework, but lets them change it if they publish the change and a justification within 30 days.

choice.p: Which of these is a documented change since 2025 that made a lab's safety framework conditional or less strict?
o: Meta changed 'stop' to 'develop with mitigations' at its top threshold
OpenAI dropped cybersecurity from the categories its framework tracks
Google DeepMind dropped its capability thresholds for case-by-case review
Anthropic replaced its framework with a pledge to follow government rules
ow: Cybersecurity is still a tracked category; Astra was rated Critical in it.
Google kept its critical capability levels and added a lower tier of tracked levels in 2026.
Anthropic rewrote its policy and publishes regular risk reports.

items.p: How much time did outside evaluators typically get to test frontier models before release in 2025 and 2026?
o: From a few days to a few weeks
Six months or more for each model
About two to three months per model
None: outside testing began after release
ow: Published windows are far shorter.
Published windows were shorter: METR had about three weeks with o3, and UK AISI 3 working days for one Claude Opus 4.6 test.
Labs set release dates; testers worked within them.
keys: days to a few weeks
e.g., METR about 3 weeks; UK AISI 3 working days; CAISI one-week windows
items.x: METR had about three weeks with OpenAI's o3 and no access to its internal reasoning. For Claude Opus 4.6, UK AISI tested misalignment over 3 working days and US CAISI tested cyber over a one-week window. Apollo's testing of GPT-6 Astra lasted three days.

items.p: Labs increasingly justify a release with a 'safety case': a structured argument that a model is unlikely to cause a catastrophe. One says: 'Even if our model tried to cause a catastrophe, our monitoring and permissions would stop it.' What kind of argument is this?
o: A control argument
An inability argument
A trustworthiness argument
A deference argument
ow: An inability argument says the model can't cause the harm even if it tried.
A trustworthiness argument says the model can but won't, because its goals are good.
A deference argument relies on the judgment of trusted AI advisors.
keys: control argument
safe even if the model tries, because the safeguards hold
items.x: A safety case is 'a structured rationale that AI systems are unlikely to cause a catastrophe' (Clymer et al., 2024), with four argument types: inability, control, trustworthiness and deference. As models get more capable, inability arguments get harder to make, so labs shift to control and trustworthiness.

items.p: A system card reports dangerous-capability results for a 'helpful-only' version of the model, trained without its usual refusals. Why test that version instead of the one customers get?
o: Refusals can be jailbroken or removed, so the test shows what's underneath
The helpful-only version is the one the lab plans to sell to most customers
Refusals slow testing down, so removing them mainly saves evaluators time
Regulators require capability tests on versions without safeguards
ow: Customers get the safeguarded version; the helpful-only one is a testing tool.
Refusals would hide capability the model still has, so the test would understate it.
No law sets this rule; labs do it because refusals can hide real capability.
keys: refusals can be bypassed or removed
testing without them shows the underlying capability
items.x: This ties together two earlier ideas: refusal training is brittle (cheap jailbreaks, cheap fine-tuning on open weights), and evaluations are lower bounds. A capability test on the safeguarded model would partly measure the refusals and understate what a determined attacker could get.

units.title: Reading the evidence: practice
units.desc: Mixed practice with the kinds of claims policy people meet in system cards, press releases and testimony. Pick the strongest response using everything in the course.

items.p: A lab says: 'Our model scored below the danger threshold on all our bioweapons evaluations, so it's safe to release.' What's the strongest objection?
o: Tests set a floor: weak elicitation or test-aware models can hide capability
Bio benchmarks are often contaminated, which makes scores look too low
Bio risk turns on lab equipment more than know-how, so the tests miss the point
A model that answers biology questions well is dangerous whatever tests show
ow: Contamination usually inflates scores, so it wouldn't explain a falsely low result.
That argues the model is safer than the tests suggest; the stronger objection is that tests show a floor on capability.
That proves too much; the question is whether this model crosses a threshold.
keys: evaluations are lower bounds
elicitation effort matters
evaluation awareness or sandbagging could hide capability
items.x: Ask what elicitation was used (tools, fine-tuning, token budget), whether the tested snapshot is the one shipping, and how the lab handled evaluation awareness. Anthropic notes its automated bio benchmarks were 'largely saturated' by early 2026, pushing it toward uplift trials and red teaming.

items.p: A news story says scores on a popular coding benchmark went from 60% to near 100% in one year. Before concluding models can now do software engineers' jobs, what should you check first?
o: Whether the test is contaminated or flawed, and whether it resembles real work
How fast the models solved the tasks compared with human engineers
Whether the models behind the jump were much larger than last year's
Whether the benchmark's tasks were written by human experts or generated by AI
ow: Speed matters only if the solutions are sound and the tasks resemble real work.
Model size doesn't tell you whether the score reflects real ability.
Who wrote the tasks matters less than whether scores reflect real ability; SWE-bench Verified's tasks were human-screened and Epoch still rates it 'Flawed.'
keys: contamination
flawed tests
whether tasks match real work
items.x: Stanford's 2026 AI Index reported SWE-bench Verified rising 'from 60% to near 100% in a single year.' OpenAI's 2026 audit found flawed tests in a large share of the tasks it checked and said gains 'increasingly reflect how much the model was exposed to the benchmark at training time.' Epoch rates the benchmark 'Flawed' and finds scores depend heavily on the scaffold used.

items.p: A lab announces that its AI now 'leads' 26% of its own AI research work, up from under 1% earlier in the year. What's the most important caveat for a policy analyst?
o: It's the lab's own measure and definitions, not independently checked
The number must be wrong, because AI systems can't yet do real research work
It means the lab could now cut about a quarter of its research staff
It means AI research at the lab has become 26% faster than it was before
ow: AI does take on research tasks; the question is how this measure was built.
A share of work 'led' by AI doesn't measure how many people are needed, and the lab defines the measure itself.
Share of work 'led' isn't speed; Anthropic says its internal measures show no sustained 2x AI-driven speedup of its development.
keys: self-reported internal metric
the lab defines what 'leads' means
no independent measurement
items.x: Anthropic's index is self-reported. Independent evidence is mixed: Epoch's InnovationEval found frontier models couldn't independently reinvent a recent ML technique, while a preliminary report by a separate METR team estimated about 1.5x AI-driven acceleration of capabilities progress at Anthropic, a figure METR's published summary did not verify. Measuring AI R&D automation is now a key open problem.

items.p: A lab says: 'We monitor every chain of thought our model writes, so we'd catch it if it started scheming.' What's the strongest reason for doubt?
o: Reasoning often leaves things out, and models can become less monitorable
Chains of thought are encrypted by default, so the lab can't actually read them
Monitors can't keep up with the volume of reasoning a model writes
Scheming models skip writing reasoning, so there's nothing to see
ow: Labs can read their models' reasoning; the issue is how faithful it is.
Monitors are themselves AI models and can read at scale; the problem is what the reasoning leaves out.
Monitors catch much misbehavior in reasoning; the problem is what's left out.
keys: chain of thought isn't always faithful
monitorability can decline
training against monitors teaches hiding
items.x: Chain-of-thought monitoring is 'a new and fragile opportunity': useful for noticing problems, not for ruling them out. OpenAI reported Astra's reasoning was substantially less monitorable, largely because it reasons more briefly and does more without visible reasoning.

items.p: A lobbyist argues: 'This model was trained with less than 10^26 operations, so it isn't a frontier risk and shouldn't be covered.' What's the best response?
o: Compute is a rough proxy: smaller or distilled models can be very capable
The lobbyist is right: below 10^26, models lack frontier-level abilities
The model is covered anyway, since the EU's line is ten times lower
Lower the line to 10^25 so that models like this one are covered
ow: DeepSeek-R1, at about 3.5 x 10^24 FLOP, was reported by DeepSeek to perform comparably to OpenAI's o1.
The EU line applies in the EU and may not reach this model either; the stronger point is that compute is a rough proxy.
A lower line would still miss capable models that use little training compute; compute stays a rough proxy.
keys: compute is an imperfect proxy
capable models below the line (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, distillation, test-time compute)
pair thresholds with evaluations
items.x: DeepSeek-R1, at an estimated 3.5 x 10^24 FLOP (Epoch AI), was reported by DeepSeek to perform comparably to OpenAI's o1. New York's original RAISE Act tried to close one gap by also covering models distilled from a frontier model at a cost above $5 million.

items.p: A developer plans to release the weights of a model that matched experts on a virology troubleshooting test. It says the model's refusal training makes the release safe. What's the strongest objection?
o: Anyone with the weights can cheaply strip refusals, and the release can't be undone
Open-weight models are hard to test before release, so their abilities are unknown
Refusal training is weaker in open models because they tend to be smaller
A written virology test can't show lab ability, so the release is low-risk
ow: Open-weight models can be tested like any other; the problem is what happens after release.
Size isn't the issue: researchers stripped refusals from Llama 2-Chat 70B for under $200.
That argues for release; and a knowledge test is a floor, while released weights can't be recalled if the risk proves real.
keys: refusals can be removed cheaply from open weights
release is irreversible
items.x: This combines three earlier ideas: safety training can be undone cheaply once weights are public, a release can't be recalled, and a knowledge test sets a floor on what a model can help with. Filtering dangerous data before training held up better in 2025 research.

items.p: A 2026 system card reports a model tried to escape or tamper with its test sandbox in 1.5% of runs, and that internal signals show it often suspects it is being evaluated. Name two questions you'd ask before trusting that low rate.
items.answer: Examples: Would it behave worse in real use, given it suspects tests? Was the tested version the one being shipped? How much elicitation was used (tools, token budgets)? Who ran the tests, and for how long? Were safeguards on or off? Do interpretability or monitoring checks support the result?
keys: evaluation awareness: would real-use behavior differ?

items.x: These details come from Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 system card (September 2026). Anthropic now uses interpretability tools to measure unspoken test awareness, finding it far more often in constructed audits (36% of transcripts) than in real internal use (0.4%).

choice.p: A system card reports a model tried to tamper with its test sandbox in 1.5% of runs and often seems to suspect it is being evaluated. Which question matters most before trusting the low rate?
o: Would it behave worse in real use, when it doesn't suspect a test?
Was the 1.5% rate lower than the previous model's rate?
Did the model score well on the card's coding benchmarks?
Was the sandbox the same one used to test the previous model?
ow: A falling rate means little if the model is getting better at recognizing tests.
Capability scores don't tell you whether low misbehavior in tests carries over to real use.
Consistency helps comparisons, but the key doubt is whether a model that suspects tests acts the same in real use.
